extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (early modern metaphysics/epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining Locke's conceptual rules about how the mind forms ideas of substances, collective ideas, and relations — i.e., what constitutes our ideas of body, spirit, God, collections, and relations and how we acquire them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific ideas of substances (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our SPECIFIC ideas of substances are nothing else but A COLLECTION OF CERTAIN NUMBER OF SIMPLE IDEAS, CONSIDERED AS UNITED IN ONE THING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke illustrates with examples (e.g. 'swan' = white colour, long neck, red beak, black legs, whole feet, size, swimming power, noise, etc.). The idea of any particular substance is a compound made by uniting simple sensible ideas into a single representational subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of spiritual substances as clear as bodily substances
rubrics_metrics.description: By simple ideas from reflection (thinking, understanding, willing, perceiving, power of beginning motion, etc.) we can form the COMPLEX IDEA OF AN IMMATERIAL SPIRIT, as clear and distinct as our idea of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that putting together the ideas of thinking, perceiving, liberty, and power of moving gives as clear a notion of an immaterial spirit as assembling extension, solidity, and mobility gives of matter. The text explains construction-by-composition from simple ideas and rebuts senses-only prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: No idea of abstract substance
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no distinct idea of the substance (either of body or spirit) beyond the complex of sensible or reflective qualities; our idea of substance is obscure or possibly none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book emphasizes that the notion of 'substratum' or substance as the support of qualities is presumed but not clearly understood; even familiarity with material qualities does not yield a clearer idea of substance than we have of immaterial spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ideas peculiar to body
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary ideas peculiar to body are the COHESION OF SOLID, AND CONSEQUENTLY SEPARABLE, PARTS, and a POWER OF COMMUNICATING MOTION BY IMPULSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats figure and other qualities as consequences of finite extension; cohesion and impulse are singled out as the original ideas proper to body. He uses these to contrast bodies with spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ideas peculiar to spirit (thinking and motivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas belonging and PECULIAR TO SPIRIT are THINKING, and WILL, or A POWER OF PUTTING BODY INTO MOTION BY THOUGHT, and LIBERTY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that minds can put bodies into motion or forbear, analogous to bodies communicating motion by impulse. He also notes existence, duration, and mobility are common to both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirits are capable of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobility belongs to spirit: finite spirits operate at several times in several places and are capable of changing place (motion), just as bodies are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues from the internal experience of the soul acting on a body in the same place and being united to the body during travel (Oxford to London) to attribute motion/change-of-position to the soul; he excludes the infinite Spirit (God) from this attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: God immoveable because infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion cannot be attributed to God not because He is immaterial, but because He is infinite; the notion of 'in loco' vs 'ubi' does not affect Locke's claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a boundary claim distinguishing finite spirits (capable of motion) from the infinite divine being, which is not sensibly located or movable in the same sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison: complex idea of spirit vs body
rubrics_metrics.description: Our complex idea of BODY (extended solid substance with impulse) and of SOUL (immaterial substance that thinks and moves bodies by willing) are to be compared and found equally obscure in their substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke contends that if people find thinking mysterious, they should consider the equal obscurity in understanding extension and cohesion in bodies; both are composite of simple ideas and both rest on a supposed substratum unknown to us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion of solid parts as incomprehensible as thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding how solid parts cohere (even at micro/atomic scales) is as hard as understanding how the soul thinks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses arguments about cohesion, limits of microscopy, and how particles of water unite on cooling to show cohesion's cause is not intelligible and thus not a stronger reason to reject immaterial thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambient fluid/pressure cannot explain cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure of any ambient fluid (e.g., aether) cannot intelligibly account for cohesion of solid parts, particularly against lateral separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke provides the lateral-sliding thought experiment (polished marbles) showing ambient pressure cannot prevent sliding separation, hence fails as a general explanation for internal cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of coherence of atoms incomprehensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one explained cohesion of macroscopic bodies, one would still lack an account for the cohesion/internal bonds of the smallest particles (aether corpuscles), so extension remains unintelligible in fundamental respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke points out that hypothesizing finite or infinite matter does not make cohesion intelligible; the problem recurs at ever-smaller scales and remains obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of motion by impulse or by thought equally unintelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although experience shows motion is produced both by impulse and by thought, the manner by which motion is passed or produced (in either case) remains obscure and incomprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that even ordinary conservation-like cases (equal motion lost/gained) only give the notion of motion passing but not an intelligible mechanism; likewise, mind-caused motion is mysterious. He suggests both are on equal epistemic footing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary: sensation and reflection as limits of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation convinces us of extended substances; reflection convinces us of thinking substances; beyond simple ideas from these sources, our faculties cannot discover the underlying nature or causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke frames the central epistemological point: our ideas of substances are bounded by what sensation and reflection supply; inquiries into substrata or deeper natures lead only to ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex idea of God formed by enlarging simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our complex idea of the Supreme Being is formed by taking simple ideas (existence, duration, knowledge, power, pleasure, happiness) and enlarging their extent to infinity, producing the idea of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains the mental operation of 'enlarging' degrees (twice, thrice, to infinite) to construct the idea of infinite knowledge, power, duration, etc.; the idea of God is thus composed from reflective ideas plus the notion of infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new simple ideas in our ideas of spirits beyond sensation/reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: All ideas we attribute to God or other spirits (except infinity) derive from the same simple ideas we have from sensation or reflection; differences among spirits are degrees/extent only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes limitation: since we lack internal experience of immediate non-corporeal communication, we cannot form an idea of such communication except by analogy; all attributes we imagine are expansions of reflective/sensible ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective ideas of substances (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collective idea is one idea formed of many particular substances considered together (e.g., 'army', 'world') and is represented by the mind as one idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke characterizes collective ideas as mental compositions where the mind unites diverse particulars into a single representation; unity of an idea suffices even if it aggregates many distinct substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective ideas made by the mind's power of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind composes collective ideas by uniting several particular substances (simple or complex ideas) into one, analogous to composing numerical collective modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: troop, army, swarm, city, fleet. Locke likens this to composing numbers (a score, a gross): the mind's compositional faculty creates unified collective concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial composite things are often collective ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Many artificial things made up of distinct substances should be counted as collective ideas (e.g., army, constellation, universe), which are mental artifices bringing remote items under one conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that the mind can bring things very remote or independent into one view; collective ideas are 'artificial draughts' of the mind used for discourse and contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation defined: ideas from comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation arises when the understanding compares one thing to another, bringing two items into consideration; RELATION and RESPECT are this mental operation, and RELATIVES are denominative marks indicating that respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains how names like 'husband' or 'whiter' indicate reference beyond the primary object by pointing to another thing; any idea can be foundation of a relation, and relatives function to lead thought beyond the named subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlative vs non-correlative relative terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative terms that have clear correlatives (father/son, bigger/less, cause/effect) are obvious; where a language lacks a correlative term (e.g., 'concubine' in some tongues), the relation is less readily apprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes between readily perceived correlatives and 'external denominations' where relation exists but language does not make the correlative explicit — such relations may be less salient to speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seemingly absolute terms can conceal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words that appear to denote absolute qualities (old, great, imperfect) actually contain tacit relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke promises further discussion in following chapters; the note signals that many 'absolute' predicates imply comparison or dependence on other things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations are distinct from the things related
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea of relation can be the same among people with different ideas of the related things; e.g., 'father' is a relation superinduced on 'man' and refers to the act of generation rather than the deeper nature of the man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes that relational concepts are not reducible to the intrinsic positive content of the subjects but are comparative stances imposed by the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of relation can occur without change in the things related
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation (and consequent denomination) can cease or change purely because of a change in the other correlated thing (e.g., Caius ceases to be a father when his son dies) or by the mind's change in comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses examples to show that relation is contingent on pairing/context and that the same thing may bear contrary denominations depending on what it is compared to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation is between two things
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation involves referring or comparing two (or more) things; what is considered as one (a positive/absolute idea) is not itself a relation, though its parts may stand in relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke clarifies that a whole (e.g., triangle) is a positive absolute idea, while relations concern how parts or distinct items are set against one another.
